# Model Architecture and Encoding

Also called: NeRF Architecture, Radiance Field Network Structure, Coordinate Encoding

## Overview
Model Architecture and Encoding defines the neural network topology and input transformation functions used to map 3D spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and color. It solves the problem of representing continuous radiance fields in a differentiable manner suitable for gradient-based optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling configurations by focusing on the internal structure of the decoder (MLPs, grids, or tensors) and the mathematical formulation of the positional encoding, rather than training hyperparameters like learning rate schedules or loss weights.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map a 3D position $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and a viewing direction $\mathbf{d} \in S^2$ to a volume density $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$ and a color vector $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3$. The core mechanism involves:
1.  **Encoding:** Transforming raw coordinates into a higher-dimensional feature space using positional encoding or hash/grid lookup.
2.  **Decoding:** Passing the encoded features through a neural network (typically an MLP) to predict physical properties.
3.  **Rendering:** Integrating these properties along rays using volume rendering equations.

The specific choice of encoding (sinusoidal, hash, triplane) and network depth/width determines the model's capacity to represent high-frequency details and its computational efficiency.

## Subtopics

### [Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration](11916-depth-guided-nerf-training-configuration.md)
This configuration modifies the standard NeRF MLP by inserting dropout layers with probability $p_{drop} = 0.1$ after each of the first eight fully connected ReLU-activated layers. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly incorporating depth supervision via an Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) or similar depth loss, requiring specific weight decay ($1 \times 10^{-6}$) and learning rate schedules to handle multi-task optimization. It is chosen when ground truth depth maps are available to regularize the learning process. See [Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration](11916-depth-guided-nerf-training-configuration.md).

### [CLIPNeRF Training Configuration](12073-clipnerf-training-configuration.md)
CLIPNeRF training freezes density-related parameters $\theta_\sigma$ and utilizes patch-based rendering (128x128 pixels) to manage memory constraints while applying directional losses in the CLIP latent space. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by optimizing only color/feature parameters $\theta_c$ to achieve text-guided stylization, using a ViT-B/32 CLIP encoder. It is chosen for text-to-3D style transfer tasks. See [CLIPNeRF Training Configuration](12073-clipnerf-training-configuration.md).

### [Binary Radiance Fields](13622-binary-radiance-fields.md)
Binary Radiance Fields (BiRF) constrains feature grid parameters to binary values (+1 or -1) to achieve compact storage, replacing real-valued floating-point features with 1-bit binary features. It uses a 2D-3D hybrid multi-resolution hash architecture with a Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for gradient propagation during training. Unlike post-processing compression, BiRF performs binarization during training. It is chosen for storage-efficient radiance field representation. See [Binary Radiance Fields](13622-binary-radiance-fields.md).

### [Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture](14098-mip-nerf-360-mlp-architecture.md)
The Mip-NeRF 360 MLP architecture replaces standard positional encoding with **Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE)** to handle aliasing and frequency mismatch during volume rendering. It structures the network into two distinct MLPs: a density network (8 layers, 256 width) processing 3D spatial coordinates and a color network (1 layer, 128 width) processing view-dependent features, connected by a bottleneck vector. It is designed to be compatible with the Mip-NeRF ray integration strategy. See [Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture](14098-mip-nerf-360-mlp-architecture.md).

### [SUDS](14964-suds.md)
SUDS is a 4D radiance field representation for large-scale dynamic urban environments that factorizes the scene into three separate multi-resolution hash table branches: static, dynamic, and far-field. It distinguishes itself from siblings like [NSG](11916-depth-guided-nerf-training-configuration.md) by handling ego-motion and multi-video representations without linear memory growth per object, scaling to hundreds of square kilometers. It is chosen for large-scale dynamic scene reconstruction. See [SUDS](14964-suds.md).

### [CCNeRF](15008-ccnerf.md)
CCNeRF is a neural field representation that enables efficient compression and composition of 3D scenes by learning a hybrid tensor rank decomposition of the scene without using neural networks for rendering. Unlike NeRF variants that rely on a shared MLP renderer (e.g., NSVF) or hybrid tensor-MLP approaches (e.g., TensoRF), CCNeRF models the radiance field *only* with tensor rank decomposition, preserving low-rank approximation properties to allow dynamic model size adjustment via rank truncation and arbitrary composition via rank concatenation. It is chosen for compressible and composable 3D scenes. See [CCNeRF](15008-ccnerf.md).

### [Rip-NeRF](15532-rip-nerf.md)
Rip-NeRF is a hybrid radiance field method that renders high-fidelity, anti-aliased images by combining cone casting with anisotropic 3D Gaussian characterization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Zip-NeRF by using Ripmap-Encoded Platonic Solids to enable efficient anisotropic area-sampling, whereas Zip-NeRF relies on a multi-sampling mechanism that is effective but computationally inefficient. It is chosen for high-fidelity anti-aliased rendering. See [Rip-NeRF](15532-rip-nerf.md).

### [UE4-NeRF](15539-ue4-nerf.md)
UE4-NeRF is a neural rendering system designed for real-time interactive rendering of large-scale scenes by partitioning environments into sub-NeRFs represented as textured polygonal meshes and integrating them into the Unreal Engine 4 (UE4) rasterization pipeline. Unlike standard differentiable volume rendering which relies on ray marching, UE4-NeRF converts the learned radiance field into explicit geometry (octahedral meshes) and neural shaders, enabling frame rates up to 43 FPS at 4K resolution. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Mobile-NeRF by using regular octahedra to handle tilted surfaces and from Block-NeRF by supporting non-grid terrains, while achieving significantly faster training times through multi-resolution hash encoding. It is chosen for real-time interactive rendering in game engines. See [UE4-NeRF](15539-ue4-nerf.md).

### [Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF)](15773-generative-occupancy-fields-gof.md)
Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) is a 3D-aware image synthesis method that combines radiance fields with occupancy representations to learn compact object surfaces without impeding training convergence. It solves the problem of diffused surfaces in standard generative radiance fields (like GRAFs) and the sparse gradient convergence issues in direct occupancy networks by transitioning from cumulative volume rendering to surface-point rendering. Unlike siblings that predict volume density $\sigma$ and rely on cumulative alpha composition, GOF predicts alpha values $\alpha$ directly, reinterpreting them as occupancy to enable root-finding for precise surface location. It is chosen for high-quality 3D-aware image generation. See [Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF)](15773-generative-occupancy-fields-gof.md).

### [Panoptic Radiance Field](15849-panoptic-radiance-field.md)
Panoptic Lifting learns a panoptic 3D volumetric representation from posed RGB images and machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks, lifting noisy 2D labels into a consistent 3D representation comprising color, density, semantics, and instances. It differs from sibling methods like [Panoptic NeRF](11916-panoptic-nerf.md) and [DM-NeRF](12073-dm-nerf.md) by requiring only machine-generated 2D labels rather than manual ground truth or coarse meshes, and by explicitly modeling instance consistency via surrogate identifiers and linear assignment. It is chosen for panoptic 3D scene understanding. See [Panoptic Radiance Field](15849-panoptic-radiance-field.md).

### [Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding](15897-frequency-modulated-position-encoding.md)
Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding is a coordinate encoding scheme used in point-based radiance field optimization to map raw 3D spatial coordinates and viewing directions into a higher-dimensional feature space suitable for neural network decoding. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF positional encoding by narrowing the encoding interval (using powers of 2 with fractional exponents) to provide finer-grained basis function support for frequency modulation, which is critical for high-fidelity point cloud rendering. It serves as the input transformation stage for the AFNet MLP decoder in the FM-NeRF pipeline. It is chosen for high-frequency detail preservation in point-based rendering. See [Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding](15897-frequency-modulated-position-encoding.md).

### [MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md)
MoCo-NeRF is a framework for free-viewpoint rendering of monocular human videos that models non-rigid body motions as radiance residual fields rather than spatial offsets, using rigid skeletal transformations as a prior. It decomposes the representation into a rigid branch learning a canonical T-pose radiance field and a non-rigid branch optimizing pose-driven radiance residuals, allowing direct supervision from ground-truth pixel colors. Unlike offset-based strategies that suffer from high computational complexity and misaligned learning objectives, MoCo-NeRF reduces prediction range to the radiance space and establishes direct RGB-based supervision for both rigid and non-rigid components. It is chosen for monocular human video rendering. See [MoCo-NeRF](16197-moco-nerf.md).

### [UrbanIR](16200-urbanir.md)
UrbanIR is a method for inverse rendering of large-scale urban scenes from a single monocular video under single illumination, inferring shape, albedo, visibility, and sun/sky illumination to enable relighting and night simulation. It differs from standard NeRFs by learning intrinsic attributes (albedo, normal) independent of lighting, and from other relightable methods like NeRF-OSR or FEGR by requiring only single-illumination RGB video without LiDAR or multiple cameras. It is chosen for inverse rendering and relighting of urban scenes. See [UrbanIR](16200-urbanir.md).

#### Triplane NeRF with Diffusion Prior
The framework uses a triplane NeRF representation where scene codes are optimized jointly with a diffusion prior to handle sparse-view data and ensure end-to-end coherence [S1]. The prediction format uses v-parameterization $\hat{v}_\phi(x(t), t)$ such that $\hat{x} = \alpha(t)x(t) - \sigma(t)\hat{v}$ [S1]. The weighting function uses SNR-based weighting $w(t) = (\alpha(t)/\sigma(t))^2\omega$ instead of LSGM mechanisms [S1]. The scene code $x_i$ has shape $\mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}$, representing a triplane NeRF representation [S1]. The denoising network is a U-Net with 122M parameters [S1].

#### EG3D Triplane Representation
EG3D learns unconditional 3D-aware image generation from single-view images using a hybrid triplane representation [S2]. The triplane representation $T$ is a tensor in $\mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 96}$, corresponding to 3 axis-aligned planes (xy, xz, yz), each with 32 channels and resolution 256x256 [S2]. It renders a feature image $I_f \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 128 \times 128}$ and raw RGB image $I_{128} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 128 \times 128}$ by accumulating points along rays and performing volume rendering [S2]. A dense depth map $I_D \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 128}$ is also extracted [S2]. These are fed into a 2D super-resolution network to yield final output $I_{512} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 512 \times 512}$ via $SuperRes(I_f, I_{128}) = I_{512}$ [S2]. The rendering speed is 42 fps on RTX 3090 [S2].

#### NeRF-W Hyperparameter Configuration
NeRF-W uses an MLP architecture for modeling density and radiance [S3]. It employs 8 layers of 512 hidden units for the ‘Base’ component, and 4 layers of 128 hidden units for both ‘Static’ and “Transient / Uncertainty’ components [S3]. Positional encoding uses 15 frequencies for position and 4 for viewing direction [S3]. During training, 512 points per ray are sampled from each of the coarse and fine models for a total of 1024 points per ray, doubled to 2048 during evaluation [S3]. The latent embedding vector for appearance has dimension $n(a) = 48$, and for transient objects $n(\tau) = 16$ [S3]. The L1 regularizer multiplier is $\lambda_u = 0.01$ and the minimum importance threshold is $\beta_{min} = 0.03$ [S3]. Models are trained with Adam over 300,000 iterations with a batch size of 2048 and an initial learning rate of 0.001, decaying ten-fold every 150,000 iterations [S3]. These hyperparameters were optimized for the Brandenburg Gate scene of the Phototourism dataset and reused for remaining scenes [S3].

#### Explicit Mesh Reconstruction from Neural Fields
CodeNeRF implicitly represents the 3D structure of reconstructed objects [S4]. To obtain an explicit mesh representation, the center coordinates of a $256^3$ voxel grid are fed to the CodeNeRF MLP to obtain volume density values $\sigma$ [S4]. The Marching Cubes algorithm is applied to the volume density values $\sigma$ to find mesh vertices [S4]. Rays are cast along the vertex normals of the generated mesh to associate colors to the vertices [S4].

#### Efficient EndoNeRF scene representation
Efficient EndoNeRF is a voxel-grids-based scene representation that replaces coordinate-based MLPs with explicit density and feature volume grids to accelerate optimization [S5]. It is combined with a canonical field and time-dependent deformation field for dynamic surgical scenes [S5]. The dynamic scene at time $t$ is modeled by warping a canonical radiance field (represented by $\mathbf{V}_\sigma$ and $\mathbf{V}_a$) with a time-dependent deformation field [S5]. The deformation field is modeled using decomposed 4D motion fields and a 3-layer MLP that maps a spatial-temporal coordinate to a deformation offset [S5].

#### NeRF-Liif
NeRF-Liif is a baseline method that super-resolves LR images using a pretrained LIIF (Local Implicit Image Function) model [S6]. It requires LR-HR pairs for training and introduces external data priors [S6]. On the synthetic Blender dataset, LIIF may produce false predictions due to domain mismatch with its external training set [S6]. On the real-world LLFF dataset, LIIF tends to be oversmooth and may predict false color or geometry [S6]. Performance metrics: Blender ×2 (100x100): PSNR 27.07, SSIM 0.919, LPIPS 0.067; Blender ×4 (100x100): PSNR 25.36, SSIM 0.885, LPIPS 0.125; Blender ×2 (200x200): PSNR 28.81, SSIM 0.934, LPIPS 0.058; Blender ×4 (200x200): PSNR 27.34, SSIM 0.912, LPIPS 0.096; LLFF ×2: PSNR 26.81, SSIM 0.823, LPIPS 0.145; LLFF ×4: PSNR 24.76, SSIM 0.723, LPIPS 0.292 [S6].

#### UniSurf
UniSurf is a method unifying volume rendering (radiance fields) and surface rendering (implicit surfaces) to achieve high-quality geometry and sharp textures without mask supervision [S7, unofficial]. It uses an occupancy field where the occupancy at the $i^{th}$ sample corresponds to an indicator of surface presence [S7, unofficial]. It uses volume rendering in the early stage for optimization without mask supervision [S7, unofficial]. It uses surface rendering in the later stage to extract level-set surfaces [S7, unofficial]. Unlike pure surface rendering which requires mask supervision and has blurry texture mapping, this method provides high-quality novel views and sharp textures/colors without mask supervision [S7, unofficial].

## Background
The foundational NeRF architecture introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 established the use of a fully connected MLP with positional encoding to represent radiance fields [S1][S7, unofficial][S3]. Subsequent works have modified this architecture to address specific challenges: efficiency (Instant-NGP, BiRF), dynamic scenes (SUDS, EndoNeRF), generative capabilities (Diffusion NeRF, EG3D), and inverse rendering (UrbanIR). The evolution of encoding schemes, from standard sinusoidal positional encoding to integrated positional encoding (Mip-NeRF 360) and frequency-modulated encoding (FM-NeRF), has been driven by the need to handle aliasing and high-frequency details [S1][S7, unofficial][S3]. The shift from pure MLP decoders to hybrid grid/tensor representations (Triplane, CCNeRF) reflects the trade-off between representational capacity and computational cost [S1, S2][S7, unofficial].
